new_statements.quote: One final phonological trait, which distinguishes one dialect of Baraïn from another, is the levels of tone used. Jalkiya use three levels of phonemic tone. The wordlist for Jalking gives evidence of three levels of tone, at least phonetically. The Komiya wordlist, on the other hand, only shows evidence for two levels of tone. [p. 11:] A remarkable trait of the Jalking wordlist is that nearly every word contains at least one heavy syllable; only 14 of the 258 words do not have a heavy syllable. Of those 244 words with a heavy syllable, the first syllable of the word is heavy 232 times. It is not known if this pattern is due to a lexical restriction or if it arises from a synchronic phonological process.

new_statements.rule_in_words: Jalking is described as a tone language (three tone levels, attested at least phonetically in a 258-word list; H/M/L are marked on every wordlist item in the appendix). The paper says nothing about word stress or accent; the only prominence-adjacent observation is a phonotactic preference for a heavy word-initial syllable (232 of 258 words), which the author explicitly leaves unexplained and does not call stress.
new_statements.exceptions: None regarding stress. Tone: 14 of 258 words lack a heavy syllable; six Jalking words differ from other dialects only by initial vowel length 'and, in some cases, a change in tone' (Table 8).
new_statements.domain_note: Wordlist citation forms only (258 isolated words plus a few numbers); no phrase-level or connected-speech data; tone levels for Jalking are phonetic observations, not a phonemic analysis.
new_statements.identity_note: Glottolog saka1296 'Jalking' is the eastern Barain variety, split from Barain [bva] (bare1279) on Lovestrand's intelligibility evidence; Glottolog attaches no references to it. The only first-hand linguistic data on Jalking are in Lovestrand 2011 (SILEWP 2011-011), a four-dialect comparison of Baraïn built on a 258-item Jalking wordlist (villages Doutoum, Panchila, Djibi, Nyame area, east of Melfi); the author treats Jalking as a 'dialect' of Baraïn while noting it may be a separate language. All later Lovestrand works (2012 MA thesis, 2012 SILEWP, 2013 JWAL, 2018 DPhil, 2022 OUP, 2026 LangSci) describe the Jalkiya/Giliya lects and mention Jalking only by name; the 1996 SIL survey calls the eastern group Dakne / sakaya / jalkin-jelkin.

sources.note: Nothing: a full-text search for stress/accent|accent|prominen|pitch returns 0 hits. §3.3 Tone (printed p.10, PDF p.11): 'The wordlist for Jalking gives evidence of three levels of tone, at least phonetically'; Table 11 (p.15) summarises Jalking tone as '3 levels'. §4 (p.11) notes that 232 of 258 Jalking wordlist items have a heavy first syllable, explaining word-initial long vowels; this is presented as a phonotactic/lexical pattern, not as stress.
No references attached to saka1296; classification comment cites Joseph Lovestrand 2011 for non-intelligibility of the eastern variety; alternative names Sakaya, Dagne, Jelkin.
